    Significance test for the directed PIT-Wasserstein metric

    d_pit_significance.Rd

    Tests the null hypothesis that the predictions are calibrated. D_pit is signed, so unlike u_pit_significance() this test reports a direction: positive values indicate overconfidence (predictive distributions too narrow) and negative values underconfidence (too wide).

    d_pit_significance(
  D_pit,
  n_predictions,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "overconfident", "underconfident")
)

    Arguments

    D_pit

    the directed PIT-Wasserstein metric, as returned by pit_w() or prediction_scores()

    n_predictions

    the number of predictions each D_pit was computed from, as returned by prediction_scores()

    alternative

    one of "two.sided" (any dispersion miscalibration), "overconfident" (positive D_pit only) or "underconfident" (negative D_pit only) (default `two.sided `; allowed: `two.sided `,`overconfident `,`underconfident`)

    Value

    a dataframe with one row per input value and columns:

    • D_pit, n_predictions — as supplied

    • statistic — the z score, \(D^*_{pit}\sqrt{48n}\)

    • se — the null standard error, \(1/\sqrt{48n}\)

    • critical_0.05 — the magnitude of D_pit rejected at 5%

    • direction — "overconfident", "underconfident" or "calibrated"

    • p_value — computed against alternative

    Details

    D_pit is a linear functional of the empirical quantile process, so its null is exactly Gaussian with a known variance, \(D^*_{pit} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/(48n))\). No simulation, bootstrap or nuisance parameter is required.

    The normal approximation to a sum of order statistics converges from above, so for n_predictions below about 50 the test is mildly anti-conservative (empirical size around 8% at n = 10, 6% at n = 25, 5.5% at n = 50); treat small-sample p values as approximate.

    Unit tests

    

# a z score of 1.96 is a two sided p of 0.05
res = d_pit_significance(qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(48 * 100), 100)
testthat::expect_equal(res$statistic, qnorm(0.975))
testthat::expect_equal(res$p_value, 0.05)
testthat::expect_equal(res$direction, "overconfident")

# the one sided test is half the two sided test in the expected direction
testthat::expect_equal(
  d_pit_significance(0.01, 100, "overconfident")$p_value,
  d_pit_significance(0.01, 100)$p_value / 2
)

# and is not fooled by a deviation in the other direction
testthat::expect_true(d_pit_significance(-0.03, 100, "overconfident")$p_value > 0.95)

# exactly calibrated
testthat::expect_equal(d_pit_significance(0, 100)$p_value, 1)
testthat::expect_equal(d_pit_significance(0, 100)$direction, "calibrated")
